The book of Acts ended with ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧, a prisoner waiting for his case to be heard by the emperor. The letter to the Romans was written a few years before that, when Paul had never set foot in the city at all. It was a letter of introduction, sent ahead of a visit he had long hoped to make, and it became the fullest account of his gospel that he ever set down.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ was a Jew from ⟦l:tarsus_1140|Tarsus⟧, in what is now southern Turkey, trained in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ as a Pharisee and once a fierce opponent of the followers of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. On the road to ⟦l:damascus_322|Damascus⟧ the risen Jesus met him, and the persecutor became the apostle to the Gentiles. For the better part of twenty years he had carried the message about Jesus through ⟦l:syria_1122|Syria⟧, ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ Minor, ⟦l:macedonia_747|Macedonia⟧ and ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧, founding small communities of believers in one city after another. By the time of this letter that work in the eastern Mediterranean was, in his own words, complete, and he was looking west, to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ and beyond it to ⟦l:spain_1111|Spain⟧.

The letter was written from ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧, during the three months ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ spent in ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧ near the end of his third great missionary journey, in the middle fifties of the first century. The clues are in the final chapter. Paul is staying with a man named Gaius, who hosts the whole church. Greetings come from ⟦p:erastus_1213|Erastus⟧, the city treasurer. And the woman who carried the letter, Phoebe, serves the church at Cenchrea, the eastern harbour of Corinth. A secretary named Tertius wrote it down as Paul dictated.

The church in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ was not ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s. Visitors from Rome were in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ on the day of Pentecost, and Jewish travellers and traders moved constantly between the capital and the east. The believers met in households scattered across the city, and they included both Jews and Gentiles. Some years earlier the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome, an event Acts mentions in passing, because it brought the Jewish couple ⟦p:priscilla_2370|Priscilla⟧ and ⟦p:aquila_279|Aquila⟧ to ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧, where they became Paul's friends and fellow workers. By the time of this letter they were back in Rome. Jewish and Gentile believers now shared the life of the church in the capital, and the letter shows that belonging together did not always come easily to them. Nero was emperor, still in the early and relatively peaceful years of his reign.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ had several reasons to write. He wanted the Roman believers to know him and his message before he arrived, and to support his mission to ⟦l:spain_1111|Spain⟧. His teaching had been misrepresented, and some claimed that his gospel of grace encouraged people to sin, so he lays out what he actually proclaims, carefully and at length. He was also about to set off for ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ with a gift of money collected from the Gentile churches of ⟦l:macedonia_747|Macedonia⟧ and ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧ for the poor believers in ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧, and he was anxious about how it would be received. Behind all of these lies one great question: how Jews and Gentiles belong together in the one people of God, and what has become of God's promises to Israel now that the Messiah has come and so many of Israel have not believed in him.

The letter moves like a sustained argument. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ begins by showing that the whole human race, Gentile and Jew alike, stands guilty before God. He then announces that God has provided a righteousness of his own, received through faith in ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, and he calls ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ as his witness. From there he traces what this means: peace with God, freedom from the reign of sin and death, life in ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧, and a hope that nothing in all creation can take away. In the central chapters he wrestles with the unbelief of his own people and the faithfulness of God. Only then does he turn to how the believers in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ should live, toward one another, toward the authorities, and across their differences over food and holy days. He closes with his travel plans and a long, warm list of greetings.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ did reach ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and there he was arrested. When he finally came to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧, about three years later, it was in chains. Believers from the city, the church to which this letter had been read aloud, came out along the Appian Way to meet him.
1:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ opens in the formal style of an ancient letter, writer first and then recipients, but he stretches the opening greeting into a compact summary of his message. He is a servant of Christ ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, called to be an apostle, and the gospel he serves was promised long ago through the prophets. It concerns God's Son, a descendant of ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, declared with power to be the Son of God by his resurrection.

He then turns to the believers in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ personally. He thanks God that their faith is spoken of everywhere, and he explains that he has often planned to come to them and been prevented. He is eager to preach in Rome too, because he is not ashamed of the gospel. It is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, the Jew first and also the Greek, and in it the righteousness of God is revealed.

Then the tone changes sharply. Before ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ can explain that good news, he sets out the problem it answers, and he begins with a world that knew enough of God from creation to honour him and turned instead to idols. The picture that follows is dark, and deliberately so.
2:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has just described a world turning from God to idols and every kind of wrongdoing. Now he imagines someone listening with approval, and he turns to address that person directly. Anyone who passes judgment on others while doing the same things, he says, has no excuse.

It is the voice of a teacher in full flow, turning on an imagined listener, voicing his objections and answering them, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ will return to it again and again in this letter. At first the listener could be anyone who judges. Then, as the chapter goes on, the figure comes into focus: a fellow Jew, confident in the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, proud of circumcision, sure of being a guide to the blind and a light to those in darkness.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s point is that God shows no favouritism. He will judge every person according to what they have done, and having the law is not the same as keeping it. The chapter ends with a redefinition that would have startled many of his first hearers, of what it truly means to be a Jew.
3:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has been pressing his fellow Jews hard. Possessing the law and bearing the mark of circumcision, he has said, does not protect anyone from God's judgment. That raises an obvious objection, and the chapter opens with it. Is there any advantage in being a Jew at all?

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s answer is yes, much in every way, above all because Israel was entrusted with the very words of God. But he refuses to let that answer become a shelter. In a quick exchange of questions, some of them echoing what his critics have said about him, he insists that God remains faithful and just even when people are not. Then he gathers a chain of quotations from the Psalms and ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ to bring his whole case to its conclusion: Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin, and no one will be declared righteous by keeping the law.

Then comes the turn the letter has been waiting for, marked by two words: but now. In a dense and carefully built passage, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ announces what God has done in Christ ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ to answer the problem he has spent nearly three chapters describing.
4:
Justified by faith, apart from the works of the law, and on the same terms for Jew and Gentile: that was the claim at the close of chapter three. A Jewish reader would naturally ask how this fits with Israel's own story, and especially with ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧, the father of the nation.

So ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns to Genesis, and to the sentence from chapter fifteen that stands at the heart of his argument: ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧ believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. He adds a word from ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ in the Psalms, about the blessing of the one whose sins are forgiven. Then he makes an observation about timing. Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, years before the sign of the covenant was given. That makes him the father of uncircumcised believers as well as circumcised ones.

The chapter ends with a portrait of ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧'s faith: a man of about a hundred, with a wife long past childbearing, holding on to God's promise that he would become the father of many nations.
5:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has finished his case. Every human being stands guilty before God, and God has provided righteousness as a gift, received by faith, as it was for ⟦p:abraham_58|Abraham⟧. Now he begins to explore what follows from it.

The first thing is peace with God. Those who have been justified now stand in grace, and they can face even suffering with hope, because God has poured his love into their hearts through the Holy Spirit. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ then reflects on what kind of love this is, shown to people while they were still sinners and enemies.

In the second half of the chapter ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ widens the view to the whole of human history. He goes back to ⟦p:adam_78|Adam⟧, the first man, through whom sin and death entered the world. He sets Adam and Christ side by side, two men whose single acts have consequences for all who belong to them. The comparison is close and carefully argued, and it closes with a sentence that will provoke the question of the next chapter: where sin increased, grace increased all the more.
6:
The last chapter closed with a bold sentence: where sin increased, grace increased all the more. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ knows how that can be heard, and indeed he has been accused of teaching it. If grace is so abundant, why not go on sinning, so that there is even more of it?

His answer draws on baptism, the rite by which every believer in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ had entered the church. To be baptised into Christ, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ says, is to be joined to his death and to share in his new life. A person who has died with Christ cannot simply carry on living in the old way.

In the second half of the chapter he changes the picture. Everyone in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ knew what slavery was; a large part of the city's population were slaves or former slaves. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ uses that everyday reality, apologising as he does so for speaking in such human terms. Everyone serves some master, he says, and he contrasts the two masters a person may serve, and the wages each one pays.
7:
Believers have died with Christ, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has said, and been set free from slavery to sin. Now he turns to a related question that has hovered over the whole letter: what about the law of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧?

He begins with an illustration from marriage, aimed at those who know the law. A woman is bound to her husband only as long as he lives; once he has died, she is free to marry another. In the same way, believers have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that they may belong to the one who was raised from the dead.

That raises another question. If the law stirred up sin, is the law itself sinful? ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ answers with an emphatic no, and then speaks in the first person, of a struggle between wanting to do good and failing to do it. He delights in God's law, yet finds himself doing the very thing he hates. The chapter ends with a cry of anguish, followed at once by thanks to God.
8:
The previous chapter ended with a cry: who will rescue me from this body of death? ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s answer opens this chapter. There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧.

This chapter is one of the high points of the letter. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has said little about the Holy Spirit so far; now he speaks of ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ again and again. The Spirit gives life where the law could not. The Spirit makes believers children of God, able to call God Abba, the Aramaic word a child would use for father. And the Spirit is the firstfruits of a future that reaches beyond them to the whole creation, which Paul pictures groaning as if in childbirth while it waits to be set free.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ does not pretend that the present is easy. His readers face suffering, and he names it honestly. But the chapter builds steadily toward its close, a series of questions and answers that ends in one of the most famous passages Paul ever wrote, about the love of God in Christ, from which nothing in all creation can separate those who belong to him.
9:
Chapter eight closed in confidence: nothing in all creation can separate God's people from his love. But that confidence raises a painful question, and it brings ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ to a sudden change of tone. If God's promises are so sure, what has happened to Israel? Most of Paul's own people have not believed that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is the Messiah.

This chapter begins a section of three chapters that answers a question the letter has raised since its opening lines, where the gospel came to the Jew first. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ opens with grief, and a list of everything that belongs to Israel: the covenants, the law, the temple worship, the patriarchs, and the Messiah himself.

His first answer is that God's word has not failed. He traces Israel's history through ⟦p:isaac_616|Isaac⟧, the child of the promise, through ⟦p:israel_682|Jacob⟧ rather than ⟦p:esau_1216|Esau⟧, and God's dealings with ⟦p:pharaoh_2331|Pharaoh⟧, to show that God's purposes have always moved by his own choosing and mercy. The argument is demanding, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ expects objections. He ends with Gentiles who have found righteousness by faith, and Israel stumbling over the stone laid in ⟦l:zion_1263|Zion⟧.
10:
⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ is in the middle of his reflection on Israel's unbelief. He has argued that God's word has not failed, and that Israel stumbled because it pursued righteousness by works rather than by faith. Now he begins again with his own heart: his deepest desire and prayer is that his people may be saved.

He grants that they are zealous for God, but says their zeal was not based on knowledge. At the centre of the chapter he takes words of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ from Deuteronomy, about God's command being near, in the mouth and in the heart, and he reads them as a description of the message of faith now being proclaimed. Anyone who confesses ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ as Lord and believes that God raised him from the dead will be saved, and in this there is no difference between Jew and Greek.

The second half follows the message as it goes out to be heard. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ anticipates the excuses that might be made for Israel, that they never heard or never understood, and answers each one with Scripture, from ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ and the Psalms. The chapter ends with God holding out his hands all day long to a disobedient people.
11:
Chapter ten ended with God holding out his hands to a disobedient people. The natural question follows, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ asks it himself: has God rejected his people? His answer is immediate. Certainly not. Paul himself is an Israelite, of the tribe of ⟦p:benjamin_463|Benjamin⟧.

He recalls ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧, who once thought he was the only faithful one left in Israel, and was told that God had kept seven thousand who had not bowed to ⟦p:baal_573|Baal⟧. So now, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ says, there is a remnant chosen by grace. And Israel's stumbling is not the end of the story. Through it salvation has come to the Gentiles, and Paul hopes that it will provoke his own people to jealousy and win some of them back.

Then he speaks directly to the Gentile believers in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧. Using the image of an olive tree, he warns them against arrogance toward the Jewish people. Some natural branches have been broken off, and wild branches grafted in, but the root still holds them all. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ then speaks of a mystery about Israel's future, and the chapter ends in a hymn of praise to the unsearchable wisdom of God, which closes the whole first part of the letter.
12:
With the hymn of praise at the end of chapter eleven, the great argument of the letter is complete. For eleven chapters ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ has set out what God has done in Christ, for Jew and Gentile alike. Now, with a single word, therefore, he turns to how the believers in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ are to live in response.

The appeal is grounded in what came before. In view of God's mercy, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ urges them to offer themselves to God as living sacrifices, a striking phrase for people who knew animal sacrifices from both the temple in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and the pagan altars of ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧. He asks for a renewed way of thinking, no longer shaped by the pattern of the present age.

Much of the chapter concerns the life of the community. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ uses the picture of a body with many members, each with its own gifts, to describe how the believers belong to one another. Then comes a rapid series of short instructions about love, hospitality and humility, which extends even to how they should treat those who persecute them.
13:
The last chapter described life within the community of believers, and ended with how they should treat enemies and persecutors. Now ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns outward, to their relationship with the governing authorities.

For readers living in the imperial capital, this was no abstract question. The authorities were close at hand: the officials, the tax collectors, the soldiers of the emperor. Some years earlier imperial power had driven the Jews out of the city. Nero was now on the throne, and his reign had not yet turned to the persecution of Christians that would come within a decade. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ tells the believers to submit to the authorities as servants appointed by God, and to pay their taxes and give respect where it is due.

From what they owe the state he moves to the one debt that can never be fully paid, the debt of love, which sums up the commandments. The chapter closes with a sense of urgency. The night is nearly over and the day is near, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ calls the Roman believers to wake up and live as people of the daylight.
14:
After the broad instructions of the last two chapters, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ takes up a specific problem among the believers in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧.

Among the believers in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧, not everyone ate alike. One person's faith allowed him to eat anything; another, whose faith ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ calls weak, would eat only vegetables. One kept certain days as special; another treated every day alike. And each was tempted to look down on the other, the one with contempt, the other with condemnation.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ himself is convinced in the Lord ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ that nothing is unclean in itself. Yet he does not use the chapter to win the argument. Every one of them belongs to the same Lord, and every one will stand before God's judgment seat. So he tells them to stop judging one another, and he asks something harder of those with the freer conscience: never to let what they eat destroy a brother for whom Christ died.
15:
The disagreement between the strong and the weak over food and holy days runs on into this chapter. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ opens by including himself among the strong and telling them to bear with the weak, as Christ did not please himself. He then gathers a series of passages from the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms, all of which speak of the Gentiles praising God alongside his people. It is a fitting close to a letter so concerned with Jew and Gentile together.

Then ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns to his own plans, and the letter becomes personal again. He describes his work so far, from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ all the way around to Illyricum, on the Adriatic coast, and his ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named. Now he means to go to ⟦l:spain_1111|Spain⟧, visiting ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ on the way.

First, though, he must go to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, carrying the gift collected by the churches of ⟦l:macedonia_747|Macedonia⟧ and ⟦l:achaia_16|Achaia⟧, the province of southern ⟦l:greece_495|Greece⟧, for the poor believers there. He asks the Romans to pray that he will be rescued from unbelievers in ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ and that the gift will be accepted. Acts tells us how those prayers were answered: ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ did reach Jerusalem, and there he was arrested.
16:
The argument and the travel plans are complete, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ ends with people. The final chapter is one of the longest lists of names in the New Testament, and it offers a rare glimpse of an early church.

First comes Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchrea, the eastern port of ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧. She is carrying the letter, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ asks the Romans to welcome and help her. Then come greetings to some two dozen people by name, and to households and house churches besides. Among them are ⟦p:priscilla_2370|Prisca⟧ and ⟦p:aquila_279|Aquila⟧, the couple known in Acts as ⟦p:priscilla_2370|Priscilla⟧ and Aquila, who had worked alongside Paul in Corinth and ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧ and had now returned to ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧, with a church meeting in their house. The list includes women and men, Jews and Gentiles, and a number of names common among slaves and freed slaves.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ adds a brief warning about those who cause divisions. Then greetings come from those with him in ⟦l:corinth_306|Corinth⟧, including ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧, his host Gaius, ⟦p:erastus_1213|Erastus⟧ the city treasurer, and Tertius, who adds his own line as the one writing the letter down. It closes with a final ascription of glory to God.
